7. Dissatisfied with the appellate judgment the plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No. 1337 of 1993 to the High Court Division which set aside the judgment of the appellate court and restored that of the trial court. The High Court Division was of the view that Ext. 4, the pattani register which was called for by the plaintiff and proved by PW4, an employee of Government, had presumption of genuineness and this proved the lease in favour of the plaintiff. The High Court Division went on to say 'The learned Additional District Judge did not notice that this Pattani book is the registry of the tenants who were given pattani of lands on 1st Baishakh. 1347, on the basis of hukumnamas or like as was then the custom of the landlords. The Government could have produced all the hukumnamas or like granted on that date to show that there are no hukumnamas or like in favour of the persons mentioned in the pattani book and so presumption of fact goes against the Government." 

 10. Mr. B. Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney General, __appearing on behalf of the appellants urges that the High Court Division wrongly gave the onus of proof of the alleged settlement upon the defendants and has drawn an incorrect presumption of genuineness of Ext. 4, the pattani register, called for by the plaintiff and proved by P. W, 4. 

 15. The High Court Division had not much to find fault with the reasoning’s of the appellate court except differing in views respecting Ext. 4, an extract of the pattani register of which a certified copy was filed by the plaintiff calling for the original. It reversed the appellate judgment in consideration of Ext. 4, missing the vital aspects of Ext. 4 which pointed to its falsity, as noticed by the appellate court. We may add that there is nothing on record to relate Ext. 4 to the settlement claimed by the plaintiff. Again, the hukumnama and other documents of settlement in favour of the plaintiff were for the plaintiff to produce. In the absence of proof of existence of the said documents the defendants also could not be supposed to be in a position to produce them. Thus the High Court Division had obviously given a wrong onus and drawn an incorrect presumption as urged by Mr. B. Hossain.
